title: Episode 121: John Quincy Adams and the Amistad Rebellion: Justice Before the Supreme Court
description:
In July eighteen thirty-nine, off the northern coast of Cuba, a dramatic revolt unfolded aboard the Spanish slave schooner La Amistad. Fifty-three Mende captives from West Africa, led by a twenty-five-year-old rice farmer named Sengbe Pieh—known to Westerners as Cinqué—broke free from their chains in the hold, found cane knives, and overpowered the crew. Sparing two Spanish navigators on the condition that they steer the ship toward the rising sun back to Africa, the captives were deceived: by day the Spaniards sailed east, but by night they steered north and west.

Weeks later, a battered, ghost-like vessel was captured off the tip of Long Island by the United States revenue cutter Washington. The Mende captives were thrown into prison in New Haven, Connecticut, charged with murder and piracy. What followed was a geopolitical and legal firestorm. The Spanish Crown demanded the captives be handed over for execution, and President Martin Van Buren, desperately seeking Southern votes in the election of eighteen forty, colluded with the Spanish minister, secretly docking a federal naval warship in New Haven harbor to hustle the Africans out of the country before the courts could grant them liberty.

Abolitionists Lewis Tappan and Roger Sherman Baldwin appealed to former President John Quincy Adams to join the defense. At age seventy-three, having not argued a case before the Supreme Court in thirty years, Adams agreed. In an electrifying eight-and-a-half-hour oral argument, Adams dismantled the executive branch's unholy alliance with slave traders, invoked the Declaration of Independence, and won the unconditional freedom of the Amistad survivors. Here is George with the epic saga of justice.

FULL TRANSCRIPT:

[Rebecca - Host]
Welcome to Most Fascinating Stories. I'm Rebecca. Today, we conclude our look at President John Quincy Adams with one of the most famous civil rights cases in human history: the saga of the slave ship Amistad. In eighteen hundred and forty-one, a group of West African captives fought their way out of bondage on the high seas, only to find themselves trapped in American chains. Opposing them were the Spanish Empire and the President of the United States. Defending them was an aging former president who walked into the Supreme Court and delivered an oration that stunned the nation. Here is George with the full story.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT I: BLOOD ON THE HIGH SEAS
In the spring of eighteen thirty-nine, Portuguese slave traders kidnapped hundreds of Mende men, women, and children from their villages in modern-day Sierra Leone, in direct violation of international treaties banning the transatlantic slave trade. Packed into the suffocating, disease-ridden hold of the slave ship Tecora, they survived the brutal Middle Passage to Havana, Cuba. There, two wealthy Spanish planters, José Ruiz and Pedro Montez, purchased fifty-three captives using fraudulent passports that falsely identified them as 'Ladinos'—slaves born in Spanish colonies prior to eighteen twenty—rather than recently captured Africans. On June twenty-eighth, Ruiz and Montez loaded the captives aboard the sleek coastal schooner La Amistad, bound for their plantations in Puerto Príncipe.
On the third night at sea, a violent tropical thunderstorm lashed the vessel. In the darkness, twenty-five-year-old Sengbe Pieh, a charismatic Mende rice farmer and father of three, discovered a loose iron nail on the floor of the hold. Patiently, relentlessly, Sengbe worked the nail until he picked the padlock holding his iron collar. He freed his fellow captives. Moving silently through the hold, they discovered crates containing heavy sugarcane harvesting knives—machete-like blades two feet long.
Armed with the cane knives, Sengbe led the captives onto the main deck. In a ferocious, chaotic clash under blinding lightning, the Africans killed the captain and the ship's cook, while two Spanish sailors leaped overboard and vanished into the sea. Sengbe spared the lives of Ruiz and Montez on one strict condition: they must steer the Amistad eastward toward the rising sun, back to the shores of Africa. It was an act of justified self-defense under natural law, but the captives were about to be ensnared in a cruel deception.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT II: DECEPTION AND THE GHOST SHIP
José Ruiz and Pedro Montez were experienced mariners, and they understood that the Mende relied entirely on the sun to navigate. During the day, under the watchful eyes of Sengbe and his men, the Spaniards steered the Amistad faithfully east toward Africa. But as soon as night fell and the stars emerged, Montez quietly turned the wheel, tacking northwest toward the coast of North America.
For nearly two grueling months, the Amistad drifted across the Atlantic in a bewildering zigzag pattern. Freshwater casks ran dry, food provisions rotted, and ten of the captives died of dehydration and fever. The once-gleaming schooner became a tattered, barnacle-encrusted ghost ship, its sails shredded by gale winds and its surviving passengers emaciated to walking skeletons.
In late August eighteen thirty-nine, the Amistad finally dropped anchor off Culloden Point at the eastern tip of Long Island, New York. Sengbe and several men rowed ashore in search of fresh water and food, offering Spanish gold doubloons to local fishermen. Before they could return to sea, the United States revenue cutter Washington, commanded by Lieutenant Thomas Gedney, spotted the suspicious vessel. Gedney boarded the Amistad, took the Africans into custody at gunpoint, and towed the schooner into the harbor of New London, Connecticut.
Lieutenant Gedney was not motivated by humanitarian concern. Under maritime salvage law, he laid claim to the vessel, its cargo of textiles and gold, and the Africans themselves as valuable salvage property. The Mende survivors were transferred to the county jail in New Haven, Connecticut, charged with murder and piracy on the high seas.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT III: THE UNHOLY ALLIANCE OF WASHINGTON AND MADRID
The arrival of the Amistad in Connecticut ignited a fierce international and political firestorm. In Madrid, the young Queen Isabella II and the Spanish royal government demanded the immediate surrender of the schooner and the captives. Spain cited Pinckney's Treaty of seventeen ninety-five, which required the United States to return vessels and merchandise rescued from pirates to their rightful Spanish owners.
In Washington, President Martin Van Buren was terrified of the case. An election year was looming in eighteen forty, and Van Buren's fragile Democratic coalition depended on the support of wealthy Southern slaveholders. If the federal government freed African slaves who had murdered their white masters, Southern politicians threatened to bolt the Democratic Party, ensuring Van Buren's defeat. Van Buren ordered his Attorney General and federal prosecutors to support Spain's demands fully.
The administration engaged in shocking judicial interference. In January eighteen forty, when the federal district court in New Haven was preparing to issue its ruling, President Van Buren dispatched a federal navy schooner, the USS Grampus, to New Haven harbor. Secret executive orders were cut instructing the captain to seize the Mende captives the instant the judge ruled, hustle them onto the warship, and sail immediately for Cuba before the defense could file an appeal. To Van Buren, thirty-six innocent human lives were merely expendable currency in the game of presidential re-election.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT IV: THE ABOLITIONIST COMMITTEE AND THE TRANSLATION MIRACLE
While the White House plotted their deportation, the Mende captives found passionate defenders in New England. A coalition of evangelical abolitionists, led by New York merchant Lewis Tappan, formed the Amistad Committee to fund legal defense, provide medical care, and ensure the prisoners were treated humanely. They hired brilliant young Connecticut attorney Roger Sherman Baldwin, the grandson of founding father Roger Sherman, to lead the courtroom battle.
Baldwin faced a formidable obstacle: none of the Mende captives spoke a word of English, Spanish, or French, and no one in Connecticut spoke Mende. Without communication, the prisoners could not tell their story, refute the fraudulent Spanish documents, or explain that they were free African citizens illegally kidnapped from their homeland.
Lewis Tappan and Yale linguistics professor Josiah Willard Gibbs performed an ingenious breakthrough. Gibbs visited the New Haven jail and learned to count from one to ten in the Mende language: 'eta, fele, sau, naani, loolu...' Gibbs then traveled to the docks of New York City, wandering from wharf to wharf along the East River, reciting the Mende numbers out loud to arriving sailors. After days of searching, Gibbs struck gold on board a British naval vessel: a young West African sailor named James Covey, who had been enslaved, liberated by the British Royal Navy, and spoke both Mende and English fluently.
Covey was brought immediately to New Haven. For the first time, Sengbe Pieh and his companions had a voice. In a spellbound courtroom, Sengbe took the stand, demonstrating with visceral clarity how he and his people had been seized, chained in darkness, and starved. District Judge Andrew Judson ruled that the Africans were not Spanish subjects, had been kidnapped in violation of Spanish law, and were born free men. But the Van Buren administration appealed the decision all the way to the United States Supreme Court.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT V: THE SUMMONS TO OLD MAN ELOQUENT
Recognizing that the Supreme Court was dominated by Southern slaveholders—five of the nine justices, including Chief Justice Roger B. Taney, were from slave-owning states—Lewis Tappan knew the defense needed a champion of transcendent national stature. In October eighteen forty, Tappan traveled to Quincy, Massachusetts, to call upon seventy-three-year-old former President John Quincy Adams.
Adams was deeply reluctant. He was frail, afflicted with shaking hands, failing eyesight, and a voice that frequently cracked under strain. Furthermore, it had been more than thirty years since he had argued a case before the Supreme Court. In his diary, Adams confided his profound sense of unworthiness: 'I am not competent to the task. My faculties are in decay. My voice is broken. The world and the court have changed.'
Yet as Tappan laid out the evidence—the unholy collusion between President Van Buren and the Spanish crown, the secret deployment of the USS Grampus, and the existential threat to the rule of law—Adams felt the burning pull of duty. He wrote that he could not refuse a summons to defend innocent fellow human beings whose lives hung by a thread. He told Tappan: 'I will plead their cause before the court of my country, and if I fail, let the shame rest upon the nation, not upon my conscience.'
For four months, while continuing his duties in Congress, Adams buried himself in legal research, analyzing maritime law, treaties with Spain, the law of nations, and executive overreach. When the case of United States versus The Amistad was called on February twenty-fourth, eighteen forty-one, the Supreme Court chamber was packed to the rafters with senators, foreign diplomats, and journalists eager to witness an ex-president plead for the lives of African captives.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT VI: THE SUPREME COURT ORATION
Following Roger Sherman Baldwin's brilliant, meticulous four-hour technical argument on maritime jurisdiction, John Quincy Adams rose to deliver the closing defense. What followed across two days and eight and a half hours was one of the most magnificent forensic orations in American judicial history.
Adams did not merely argue technical statutes; he put the executive branch of the United States on trial. With righteous, blistering indignation, Adams accused President Martin Van Buren of abusing his power, perverting justice, and acting as a compliant lackey for foreign despots and domestic slaveholders. He held aloft the secret executive orders sending the USS Grampus to New Haven, calling it an act of executive tyranny designed to kidnap free men and deliver them to Spanish executioners without due process of law.
Pointing to the copy of the Declaration of Independence hanging on the wall of the courtroom, Adams commanded the justices to remember the founding truth of the republic: 'The moment you come to the Declaration of Independence, that every man has a right to life and liberty, an inalienable right, this case is decided. I ask no more in behalf of these unfortunate Africans than that which is held by every citizen of this republic as their birthright.'
In a haunting, deeply moving conclusion, Adams looked around the courtroom and reflected on his own long life. He noted that every single judge who had sat on the Supreme Court when he first argued before it thirty years earlier had passed into eternity: Marshall, Washington, Chase, Paterson. Turning to the bench, he whispered: 'I stand before you as one whose contemporaries have vanished from the earth. I too shall soon appear before the great bar of the Almighty. And I ask of you only that justice which you would hope to receive from the Judge of all mankind.'

[George - Storyteller]
ACT VII: THE VERDICT OF FREEDOM
On March ninth, eighteen forty-one, Justice Joseph Story—himself a brilliant legal scholar appointed by James Madison—delivered the majority opinion of the Supreme Court. The verdict was an overwhelming, resounding triumph for freedom.
By an eight-to-one majority, the Supreme Court ruled that the Mende captives were not slaves, but free human beings who had been illegally kidnapped in violation of international law. Justice Story wrote that the Africans were entitled to the same natural rights of self-defense as any free citizen, and had lawfully fought to regain their freedom on the high seas. The court ordered that they be discharged from federal custody immediately and declared unconditionally free.
When the news reached New Haven, Sengbe Pieh and his thirty-four surviving companions fell to their knees in tears of gratitude and joy. For the abolitionist movement, the Amistad verdict was a historic, unprecedented triumph—the first time the highest court in the United States had upheld the rights of Black Africans against the claims of white slave owners and the federal government.
The Amistad Committee raised thousands of dollars through public speaking tours, and in November eighteen forty-one, thirty-five Mende survivors, accompanied by American missionaries, boarded the barque Gentleman and sailed home to Sierra Leone. Sengbe Pieh returned to his native land a free man.
For John Quincy Adams, the Amistad victory was the crowning achievement of a legendary life. He had demonstrated that the law is not merely a tool for emperors and presidents to preserve power, but a sacred shield to protect the weak, liberate the captive, and vindicate the eternal rights of man.

[Rebecca - Host]
CONCLUSION
The Amistad case affirmed that the fundamental principles of the Declaration of Independence belong to every human being, regardless of race or nationality. John Quincy Adams's courage in the Supreme Court cemented his legacy as one of the greatest moral voices in American history. Next week, we turn to Adams's fierce political rival, America's seventh President, Andrew Jackson, and the legendary Battle of New Orleans in eighteen hundred and fifteen—where a ragtag army of backwoods riflemen, Choctaw scouts, and pirates broke the might of the British Empire. Until then, thank you for listening to Most Fascinating Stories.
